 Five must-see documentaries 
 5 Boundary-Breaking Documentaries to Watch if You Loved "You Can See Everything"
 By
 Victor Anderson 
 Nov 10, 2026 12:00 pm 
 “You Can See Everything” burst its way onto the fall movie scene and, in my books at least, has already entered the all-time discussions. It’s extremely rare for a film this popular to be this groundbreaking, let alone for a documentary. And it gets you thinking: what other documentaries this out-there languish in obscurity, waiting to be watched?
 Today, we present five documentaries that challenge what a documentary can be, much like “You Can See Everything.” They range from astonishingly simple to freewheeling insanity to elegiac poetry. Some are sad. Some are funny. Some in-between. All are utterly unique.
 "Images of the World and the Inscription of War" (dir. Harun Farocki, 1988)
 Harun Farocki’s documentary is perhaps the least assuming film on this list. There's no flashy camera or sound work, no grand new cinematic techniques, not even a score, aside from blips of classical music. Yet, it's an incredibly impactful movie about the power of imagery and perspective. Farocki travels through space and time to analyze numerous forms of image-capturing to show that even the most basic photo has a story to tell. Even a simple building diagram has a lot to say.
 “Images of the World” also might have the most in common with “You Can See Everything” thematically on this list, as they’re both focused on the subjectivity of perspective. Farocki’s film often introduces one meaning to a given image, only to double back and reveal a totally new one. 
 This comes to a head in its main discussions regarding the Holocaust and the various photographs and pictures we have from it. How does an overhead view of a concentration camp tell the story of its survivors? What does it really mean to get your picture taken? What does one singular image from your life say about you? Farocki’s film commands attention and conjures a remarkably moving portrait of what we leave behind when we’re gone.
 "Lost Lost Lost" (dir. Jonas Mekas, 1976)
 Jonas Mekas compulsively filmed his life in the same way Instagram influencers today film theirs. And, like the influencers, the raw footage of his day-to-day life probably wouldn’t make for terribly compelling cinema. But with “Lost Lost Lost,” Mekas takes on the immense task of distilling decades’ worth of home movie footage into a story of his immigrant journey in America. 
 Mekas begins as a tragically isolated figure (“I walked my heart crying from loneliness”) and becomes a thriving filmmaker within a supportive community. In tandem with his emotional arc, the film evolves in complexity, going from mere footage to interesting embellishments in sound and structure. Its philosophy may get a bit heady for some, but there’s always a beating heart in the form of Mekas, finding his place in the world.
 Many will balk at the three-hour runtime, but such a length mesmerizes you. Even if you’re checked out for most of that time, you still find yourself gripped by Mekas’ story merely by bearing witness to it. The runtime forces you to engage with the film–a shorter movie would have you just waiting for the end. This alone is a bold gambit that mainstream film wouldn’t dare to tread, but it’s also only one of the things that makes “Lost Lost Lost” a compelling watch. Get comfy. The payoff is worth it.
 "The Act of Killing" (dir. Joshua Oppenheimer, 2013)
 “The Act of Killing” caused quite a stir amongst my peers when we screened it in our documentary class, but you wouldn’t want anything less for a film this confrontational. “The Act of Killing” ruffles feathers in a way that only the bravest movies do.
 In the 1960s, the Indonesian military overthrew the government and massacred roughly a million of political enemies. 50 years later, a film crew collects some of the perpetrators and asks them to make re-enactment films of their experiences killing people. The result is a frank, stomach-churning glimpse into how humans rationalize and glorify unspeakable acts of evil.
 “The Act of Killing” bucks the moralizing instincts of traditional documentary filmmaking–there’s no narrator, no interviews with the victims, and only one title card at the very outset. We spend two hours with murderers who proudly recount and obsessively retrace the details of their crimes. But, crucially, we also see them acting normal. They joke with each other and take care of their kids right in between giving exact details of how to strangle someone without shedding blood.
 Through it all, there’s the slow, dawning realization that these actions were, to some degree, foundational to modern Indonesian society. It’s uncomfortable. Challenging. Horrifying, even. Because “The Act of Killing” is about how even the worst people imaginable are human, just like you and I. And, in some ways, we’re all capable of not just committing atrocities, but committing atrocities and thinking they’re noble.
 "Gates of Heaven" (dir. Errol Morris, 1978)
 Thanks to his seminal film, “The Thin Blue Line,” the progenitor of the entire true crime genre, Errol Morris became one of the biggest names in documentary history, but his best effort was his first. “Gates of Heaven” tells what could be the really simple story of a pet cemetery and its associates–a premise that would not be out of place in a Wright State student film, but what makes “Gates of Heaven” more than just a standard profile documentary is Morris’ admirable restraint regarding the interviewees. It turns out, you can learn a lot about people if you let them do the talking. 
 A pet cemetery proves to be a layered subject for a film, right at the intersection between universal questions of mortality and the comedy of mini-headstones emblazoned with names like “Scuffy” and “Miss Muffet.” So, too, do the quirky denizens of the surrounding towns (who would only be here for cheap laughs in any other movie) show a lot of insight into the world and their places in it. It’s told very plainly, with most of it consisting of interviews. But that’s all it needs to work its magic. Towards the end is a montage of the graves without any editorializing as to whether we’re supposed to find it funny or poignant. Morris just invites us to look as if we were visiting the cemetery ourselves.
 “Gates of Heaven” is unique amongst most documentaries in that it shows you this place and these people, but leaves the broader message up to you. Morris doesn’t need fancy camera work or lighting setups: he has people.
 "WR: Mysteries of the Organism" (dir. Dusan Makavejev, 1971)
 Ever wondered about the inner machinations of dirty magazines? Can sexual energy be harnessed to cure disease? Would communism work out if Stalin just got a little more bedroom action? All is revealed in “WR: Mysteries of the Organism,” an irreverent skewering of societal prudishness and what we arbitrarily take seriously. Director Dusan Makavejev gleefully twirls through wacko sex therapy, Russian propaganda, and fictional scenes from the class struggle in Yugoslavia to smash together one of the wildest films you’ll ever see.
 “WR” isn’t really a story as much as it is a parade of comic scenes and sequences, each more outrageous and oddly thought-provoking than the last. It's European arthouse by way of mid-2000s raunchy comedy. 
 “WR” is not a serious interrogation of sex or politics, but an interrogation of our seriousness towards sex and politics. Makavejev boldly suggests that maybe the core problem of our world is that we don’t get enough fun out of life. And you know what? Maybe he’s on to something. “WR” is an explosion of jaw-dropping ideas and gut-bustingly funny gags the likes of which you’ll never forget.
